en: He introduces the *Herukābhyudaya*: "Listen," and so forth. *Tattva* is the essential nature of cause and fruit, as well as that which will be explained by the passage beginning with "pleasure and union. The *ḍāka* is the Blessed Lord; the *ḍākinīs* are the goddesses. Regarding "Vajrasattva": having first become Vajrasattva, he is the Vajra-holder who possesses the causal vajra; then, possessing the state of vajra, he becomes the Vajra-holder who possesses the resultant vajra. This is the summary statement (*uddeśa*). Its detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*) begins with "In the moon," and so forth.

The garland of seed-syllables, *āli* and *kāli*, within the lunar disc serves for the generation of the Causal Vajradhara. By virtue of being a lunar disc, his white color is indicated. Here, the Blessed One’s generation stage (*utpattikrama*) is not explicitly shown, because it is not distinct from what precedes it. For here too, one must first meditate on the corpse and so forth, as previously described; however, in this case, the symbol is a skull-cup transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*.

In the sequence of the fivefold manifest enlightenment (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*), the syllables *hūṃ* and *āḥ* should be meditated upon as situated within a skull-cup and a flaying knife (*kartṛ*) produced from them. This is because the resultant Vajradhara arises from these two seed-syllables. It is understood that for the causal Vajradhara as well, these same two seed-syllables are the source. Having experienced the bliss of joy (*ānanda*) and so forth through the union of the churner and the churned (*manthyamanthāna-yoga*) with this consort, one should meditate on the goddesses arisen from one’s own seed-syllable, which has emerged from the drops of bodhicitta, each in their respective place.

The seed-syllables, emblems, and so forth of the goddesses, as well as the weapons and so forth of the Blessed One, should be understood to be identical to those of the fruit-maṇḍala. Having thus emanated the goddesses, through great passion, he assumes a swift form together with the goddess according to the instruction.

Then the Pukkasi and others urge him to emerge from the meditative absorption of dissolution (*vilayasamādhi*). First, the Pukkasi exhorts him: "Arise, O Blessed One! Being one whose mind is filled with compassion, protect me, the Pukkasi! How so? For the sake of great bliss—the bliss of great liberation—the yoga is the form of Hevajra arising from the fluid [of seminal essence]. With that, desire me; delight me! Abandon the state of being of the nature of emptiness and take on the form of fluidity."

Then Śabarī said: "I shall die from this separation, being deprived of you. Arise, O Vajra! Abandon the nature of emptiness and assume a liquid form; let the purpose of Śabarī be accomplished. Then Caṇḍālī said: "Having invited the world to the state of Buddhahood, O Lord of the Bliss of Union, why do you remain in the form of a liquid within emptiness? I, Caṇḍālī, make this request: what [is it]? Without you, I am bewildered; the meaning is that I see nothing but darkness."

Then the *ḍombī* says: "O magician, arise! This entire variety of forms is your magic trick. Consider us *ḍombīs* to be clever and urbane; we cannot be deceived. Therefore, do not in vain cause the severance of compassion by means of this liquid form. And in this matter, the Blessed One’s meditative absorption (*samādhi*) does not have emptiness as its sole flavor, but rather consists precisely of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*)."

Nevertheless, statements such as "abandon that which is empty by nature" should be understood as referring to the gradual attainment of emptiness resulting from the failure to accomplish the welfare of the world. Furthermore, this should be seen in the context of the goddesses' entry into the state of melting immediately after their respective exhortations, due to the subsequent statement regarding emission (*utsarga*).

Thus, immediately following the exhortation, the Blessed One, appearing in liquid form through the realization that all things are like an illusion, manifests in the form of *Āḥ* and *Hūṃ*. Thereafter, the curved knife (*kartṛ*) and skull-cup (*kapāla*) are presided over by him. Then, the Holder of the Fruit-Vajra, brandishing [the knife] and threatening [with the cup], having emerged in that very manner, emits the goddesses. In this regard, the seed-syllables of the goddesses are *gaṃ*, *caṃ*, *vaṃ*, *ghaṃ*, *puṃ*, *śaṃ*, *caṃ*, and *ḍaṃ*; these alone are the mantras for their emission.

Because of the statement, "one should emit by means of the seed-syllables," [it says] "the Lord and the Mistress. The Lord is the Blessed One; the Mistress is the Blessed Lady. The connection is that one should also emit those two by means of the two seed-syllables. He states those very two seed-syllables as *hūṃ* and *āḥ*. Regarding the phrase "by means of the two blue ones, terrifying with flames": they consist of the essence of the melted mind located within the interior of the lotus; they are "terrifying" (*karāla*) because of their blazing, and "jagged" (*dantura*), and they are "blue. The use of the instrumental case (in *jvālākarālanīlābhyām*) is in reference to the act of emission.

In that regard, after the goddesses have been dispatched and have accomplished the welfare of the world, the placement in the locations to be described hereafter is to be observed; this constitutes their absorption into the self of the Blessed One.

He demonstrates the accomplishment of the maṇḍala, beginning with "the wheel of the Mothers" and so forth. "Faces" refers to the mouths; "feet" refers to the collection of thighs, shanks, and feet. Having utterly destroyed the four Māras, he has fully trodden upon them. That destruction is described in the *Sāgarasūtra* (or perhaps the *Sāgaramatisūtra*). Therein, the destruction of the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*) is the contemplation of all phenomena as being like an illusion. The destruction of the Māra of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*) is the realization of emptiness. The destruction of the Māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*) is the non-arising and non-origination [of phenomena].

The destruction of the Devaputramāra consists in the contemplation that is free from conceit regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). In this context, Skandhamāra is Brahmā, yellow in color; Kleśamāra is Viṣṇu, black; Mṛtyumāra is Maheśvara, white; and Devaputramāra is Devendra, fair-complexioned. Regarding "of fear" (*bhayasya*), it refers to the terrifying. Because he enjoys the company of women whose nature transcends the three realms, his aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is the exuberant *śṛṅgāra* (erotic); because he overcomes the four Māras, he is the Hero (*vīra*).

He is the *bībhatsa* (the loathsome) because he wears ornaments such as garlands of human skulls or because of his nakedness. That which is an imitation of the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment, accompanied by laughter, is proclaimed as *hāsya* (the comic). He is *raudra* (the furious) because of his eyes that resemble the fierce orb of the sun risen at the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*). He is *bhayānaka* (the terrifying) because his form strikes terror into all gods and demons.

Although his essential nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), unmarked by any conceptual construction whatsoever, he possesses great compassion because he arranges the world according to its capacities through the expansion of entire series of emanations, brought forth by the force of his previous vows. He is marvelous because of the extreme loftiness that transcends the world; he is peaceful because he has stilled the mass of afflictions such as passion and because he is without beginning or end. What is this thing called "rasa" (*flavor*) which is to be tasted? How so? Regarding this, Bharata says:
"Just as people who eat food taste it when it is joined with many condiments combined with various substances and the like."

"Because men mentally relish the permanent emotions (sthāyibhāva) when they are perfected through the representation of the transitory states (bhāvābhinaya), they are therefore known as the dramatic sentiments (nāṭyarasa).
— *Nāṭyaśāstra* 6.32–33.

And all those aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), are considered to consist of these stable emotional states (*sthāyibhāva*). They are called "stable" because they persist until the conclusion of the sentiment. And these were proclaimed by Bharata as the stable emotional states: laughter, love, sorrow, anger, energy, fear, as well as disgust and wonder.
Since they bring these aesthetic flavors (rasas) to life through various modes of representation (abhinaya),
these emotional states (bhāvas) must be understood by those who perform the drama.
Because it brings the meaning face-to-face, it is therefore called *abhinaya* (representation); however,
that [representation] is considered distinct according to the variations of *sattva* (inner being) in one who possesses the external limbs (*āhārya*) and the body (*aṅga*).

In that regard, the external representation (*āhārya-abhinaya*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) consists of variegated and brilliant garments, ointments, garlands, betel, ornaments, and so forth. Among these,
there are those that are to be worn, those that are to be tied, and likewise those that are to be cast upon or placed upon [the body].
In dramatic performance, the fourfold ornament and the fivefold garland are prescribed.
An *āviddha* ornament, such as an earring (*kuṇḍala*) or the like, is that which serves as a decoration for the ears;
one should specify that waist-bands (*śroṇīsūtra*), armlets (*aṅgada*), and so forth, are to be worn as fastenings.
An anklet, a *tulākodi*, a foot-ornament (*mañjīra*), various kinds of garments,
golden threads and the like, as well as necklaces and other such items, are intended to be cast [into the fire] and offered.
Wound, spread, gathered, knotted, and likewise hanging— garlands should be known by the wise as being of these five kinds.

The *aṅgābhinaya* (bodily expression) consists of graceful movements of the limbs (*lalitāṅgahāra*), such as charming glances, the raising of the eyebrows, and side-long looks. The *vāgabhinaya* (vocal expression) is the arrangement of sweet speech.
*Sattva* is of the nature of manifestation; from *sattva*, the *bhāvas* (emotional states) arise.
Horripilation, fainting, paralysis, perspiration, change of color, trembling,
change of voice, and loss of hearing— these are designated here by eight names.
Joy, grief, fear, and cold are the causes of horripilation;
fainting occurs as the dissolution of living beings whose minds have become deluded.
Stiffness arises from excessive joy, fear, anger, and passion;
likewise, it manifests as joy, anger, fear, shame, and affection.
Trauma and congestion should be known as the causes of perspiration;
cold, anger, fear, disease, and poison are the causes of discoloration.
Trembling arises from cold or exhilaration, as well as from fever, anger, and fear;
while a change in the voice originates from delusion, intoxication, or rage.
One should know that tears arise from three causes: joy, envy, and distress.
Furthermore, those [transitory states] which are seen in one rasa and are also seen in another rasa are transitory states (vyabhicārin) produced by a deficiency of *sattva*. And they are as follows:

Despair, languor, apprehension, envy, intoxication, fatigue, indolence, dejection, anxiety, delusion, memory, intelligence, shame, fickleness, joy, agitation, numbness, pride, despondency, longing, fortitude, resentment, sleep, wakefulness, dissimulation, contentment, epilepsy, affliction, madness, death, terror, and reflection— these are the thirty-three [transitory states]. Endowed with the head, hands, waist, chest, feet, and sides, and joined with the major and minor limbs, this is the summary of the six-limbed dance.
The head, the sides, the chest, the waist, the hips, and the feet are the six major limbs (aṅga).
The eyebrows, eyes, nose, lower lip, cheeks, and chin are the secondary limbs (upāṅga).
The gaze, however, is of various kinds; therein,
some is accompanied by a smile, wonder, or astonishment, and is joined with the raising of the eyebrows and side-long glances.

A glance that appears moist and is focused on a single beloved is declared here to be born of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). It is characterized by slightly upturned eyes, with the upper eyelid partially closed and the gaze somewhat vacant.
The gaze that is even, with the outer corners expanded, and characterized by wonder is desired;
it is one whose center is fully opened, yet whose lids are never excessively closed.
That gaze, with its lashes slightly curved, always serves for the perception of touch;
with the tips of the lashes quivering and the upper lid moist and arched,
it is desired as the "bud-like" (mukula) gaze when perceiving fragrance, touch, or joy.

That gaze which is sweet, slightly contracted, accompanied by a faint smile, and likewise turned [sideways] is called *lalitā* (graceful); it is used by women when looking at someone from the corner of the eye (*ardhāvalokana*).
Such are the [various types of glances].
Thirty-six views (dṛṣṭi) are declared in the scripture as being based on the flavors of existence;
specifically, one hundred and eight instruments (karaṇa) are declared.
Furthermore, there are thirty-two types of hunger and four types of appetite.
Therefore, I have related only a small portion here for the sake of the student's proficiency;
its full detail, however, should be learned from the *Bharata-śāstra* and other such works.

Furthermore, these elements (*bhāva*) and so forth are to be understood here in this tantra according to their respective applications. Specifically, the particularities of the Blessed Ones' dance-gestures (*nṛtyākṣepa*) have been described in the *Padanikṣepa-tantra* and others, and have been treated by us in detail in the *Vajrāvalī*. Enough, then, with this digression.

"He who has made a necklace from a garland of skulls" is what is meant by that expression. *Tāṇḍava* is a fierce dance. "Terrifying" means having a black complexion in a manner that inspires fear. *Sphārayet* means "causing to expand," referring to one who is so expanding. *Vigraha* is the body. *Ratīrama* is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*). That itself is the "pair" (*dvandva*) because it possesses conceptualization (*savikalpatvāt*). "Attained to that" (*tatsamāpanna*) is because he has previously brought that [state] face-to-face. To the question, "What is to be sealed by this reality? he says: "With Nairātmyā. [This refers to] the union (*saṃpuṭa*) with Nairātmyā.

Waveless, free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), bliss is innate joy (*sahajānanda*). To one who has attained that—that is, who has reached it—he says, "By means of what reality (*tattva*) is [Hevajra] sealed? [The answer is: "He whose nature is waveless. Because he is the antidote to all conceptual proliferation, his nature is waveless; since he possesses that nature which is the form of Hevajra, he is so described. "Terrifying" (*vikarālin*) means having formidable fangs. He is enriched with eight faces and twenty-four eyes, because each face has three round, red eyes.

Immediately following this verse, one verse concerning the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others should be understood. Among all the faces, the erotic sentiment prevails; in the white [face] it is the peaceful (*śānta*), in the non-white [faces] it is the furious (*raudra*), and in the remaining [faces] it is according to their respective application. The *caṣaka* is a skull filled with intoxicant; the *kapāla* is a skull filled with blood.

"Thus is the various ritual procedure": having performed the rite of the manifestation of the Blessed One, one should place Gaurī and the others who have been released. In the two left hands of Gaurī are a bow, a Rohita fish, and a red skull-cup containing a *bhūta*. In the two left hands of Caurī are a goad, a boar, and a red skull-cup. Pramohā is a Ḍombī; in her two left hands are a jackal situated in a skull-cup containing the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the lifting of the earth with a plow. Vettālī is white, wrinkled, and yellow.

In the two left [hands] of Vāmā are a skull-cup filled with wine and urine, and in the right, a skull-cup containing blood; she has a tortoise [as her mount] and displays the *varada* mudrā. In the two left [hands] of Pukkāsī is a lion atop a skull-cup full of flesh, and she displays the *varada* mudrā. In the right [hand] of Caṇḍālī is a skull-cup containing a blood-filled corpse; she has a tiger [as her mount]. Ghasmarī is greenish-yellow. In her two left [hands] are a fire-pit marked with a vajra and a battle-axe (*paraśu*). In the two right [hands] are a serpent atop a skull-cup full of fat and the *abhaya* mudrā. In the two right [hands] of Śabarī is a mendicant atop a skull-cup containing semen and a vajra.

"One should apply and meditate upon those who possess universal forms" means according to the ritual rule (*vidhivat*). This refers to the prescription of substances such as *rohitā* and others not previously mentioned within the skull-bowls (*karoṭa*). "Ornaments" refers to the wheel (*cakra*) and so forth. Furthermore, there is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of these [goddesses] according to the sequence of their seed-syllables (*bīja*). Among them, Gaurī, Caurī, Vettālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Pramohā are characterized respectively by gentle, fierce, joyful, the act of chewing the dead, dancing, peaceful, upward-facing, intoxicated, and bewildered gazes.

They are to be visualized in the cardinal and intermediate directions—east, south, west, north, northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest—in their respective order. Regarding the color of the faces of those with horse-forms and so forth, he states it according to the sequence of the primary face, the right, the left, and the upward-facing one: "black," and so on. The lion-faced [deity] is red and stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture; this applies specifically to the gatekeepers. The other deities, however, are seated in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅkin*). The seed-syllables for the flute and so forth are, in order: *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīḥ trāṃ hāṃ trāṃ*.
And here, one should understand the empowerment of the sense faculties, the empowerment of body, speech, and mind, as well as the consecration, sealing, worship, and so forth.

As for the realization (*abhisamaya*) of this Blessed One, it is as previously described for the three Herukas; however, the distinction is as follows: within the interior of the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), according to the ritual procedure, one visualizes the two seed-syllables arising from the *hūṃ* situated between the moon and sun born from the *ālikāli*, which are located upon a skull and a flaying knife. From the total transformation of all these arises Vajrasattva, adorned with the six seals (*ṣaṇmudrin*) and distinguished by his eight faces and so forth. Then, emerging from the interior of the lotus—born from the drops of bodhicitta produced by the churning of the churner and the churned—one visualizes Gaurī and the others, arisen from the seed-syllables *gaṃ*, *caṃ*, *vaṃ*, *ghaṃ*, *puṃ*, *śaṃ*, *caṃ*, and *praṃ*.

They are to be visualized in their respective places. Then, the mind—its form interlaced with two *hoḥ* syllables—should enter into the interior of the lotus through the mouth. Thereupon, having melted due to great passion together with the consort (*vidyā*), the Vajrin, exhorted by the words "Oṭṭhe" and so forth, immediately after the entry of the goddess, transforms from that fluid state into the form beginning with *hūṃ*. He should recite: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Dharmadhātu."

Then, immediately after the application of the bases for the eyes and so forth, one should visualize a white syllable *oṃ* on the head of Nairātmyā, pervading as far as the heart by means of other subtle *oṃ*s; a black syllable *hūṃ* in the heart, likewise pervading as far as the hips; and a red syllable *āḥ* in the secret place, likewise pervading as far as the soles of the feet. *Oṃ padma sukhādhāra mahārāgasukhadada caturānandabhāg viśva hūṃ 2 kāryaṃ kuruṣva me.* (O Lotus, support of bliss, giver of the bliss of great passion, partaker of the four joys, O Universal One! Hūṃ 2! Accomplish my purpose!)

*Oṃ vajra mahādveṣa, giver of the four joys, whose singular essence is the face of the sky, O Lord, hūṃ hūṃ, perform my task!* Having thus consecrated the lotus and the vajra, and having commenced the union as before, one should emit the goddesses Gaurī and the others. Both the goddess and the Blessed One, having been emitted from the [respective] seed-syllables produced from themselves, should be meditated upon within oneself. Then, one should perform the consecration of the eyes and so forth for all of them as before.

Thereafter, one should meditate upon and recite the sequence beginning with the entry of the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*), the empowerment, the sealing, and the tasting of the nectar—namely, the supreme king of the mandala and so forth.
The ninth cluster in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*, the commentary on the *Śrīsampuṭa*.
